The Yemeni Houthis advance down Yemen's Red Sea coast toward Bab al-Mandeb, firing missiles at Saudi energy facilities and forcing Riyadh to scramble for US support, the Financial Times reports. But when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump, the response was anything but reassuring — Trump claimed the Houthis "don't want to fight" America and are "letting most ships go through."
💬 “They don’t want us to go after them,” Trump said. “They’re letting most ships go through. There’s just one country that they’re not too happy with."
The stakes for Saudi Arabia:
🔴 Saudi oil production fell to 6.2 million bpd in August — the lowest in 36 years
🔴 The kingdom is now shipping less than half as much crude as the US
🔴 The East-West pipeline closure threatens to halt refinery operations within days
🔴 The Houthis are firing missiles and drones at Saudi energy facilities
💬 "The US is not going to come in and support it," analysts say. Trump is focused on Iran, and his history with the Houthis — praising their "bravery" after a failed bombing campaign — suggests he won't intervene.
MBS faces his biggest test since [Jamal Khashoggi's murder](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/64542). And this time, Washington isn't riding to the rescue.

💣📲 Tech titans sell AI apocalypse, cash in – while real harm becomes footnotes
The architects of Silicon Valley’s AI boom - OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, and Elon Musk - are now calling for the race[ to hit the brakes](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74507?single) .
They’ve been painting a scary scenario where fast-advancing AI could eventually pose an existential threat to humanity.
Yet despite the apocalyptic narrative, the same CEOs and their companies continue to rake in profits from the tech - even as stocks dipped amid the latest doom cycle.
The public apocalypse-peddling also serves as a perfect smokescreen - to dodge accountability for the real problems AI is creating here and now.
Framing AI as an existential threat:
🔴 positions the same billionaires as responsible guardians
🔴 draws investment and attention to “AI safety”
🔴 sidelines scrutiny of the concrete, already-occurring harms 
This is hardly a new script. In 2023, hundreds of AI and tech figures signed a statement likening AI extinction risks with pandemics and nuclear war. 
At the same time, more tangible problems get brushed aside. 
[Avaricious Bilderberg globalists l](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/68229)ike Bill Gates and former Google CEO aka drone warfare advocate [Eric Schmidt](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/72215), among others, have argued that AI’s potential is simply too enormous to be constrained by concerns over its energy or environmental footprint.
The new warning from the power players comes amid growing scrutiny of AI’s current risks:
🔶 data centers consuming electricity and water on an industrial scale, while environmental costs are downplayed
🔶 [rogue-prone](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73958), [kill-chain-peddling AI](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73834) used to identify targets in war zones, assist predictive policing and reproduce discriminatory biases
🔶 artists, writers and other workers facing displacement as companies automate tasks with increasingly capable models
🔶 deepfakes, revenge porn, disinformation and cyber vulnerabilities spreading faster 
🔶 governments and corporations deploying AI-powered surveillance with limited transparency or accountability
AI is not one unstoppable entity – it is a collection of machine-learning systems with extraordinary capabilities.
Reducing all of this to an eventual Artificial General Intelligence “singularity” - the hypothetical future moment when AI surpasses human capability - lets Silicon Valley’s mouthpieces avoid hard questions about power, accountability, and present-day damage.

🔍 Pentagon admits US has ‘on-orbit’ weapons in space
For years, the US was wary of openly discussing orbital weaponry - ostensibly out of fear of fueling a global arms race.
Those claims now ring hollow.
US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink has confirmed that the United States already fields “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.” 
He also confirmed to the Air and Space Forces Association conference that:
🔴 these on-orbit capabilities “can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes”
🔴 “space control” means both protecting US assets and “negating” an adversary’s space capabilities
🔴 options range from kinetic kill vehicles to non-kinetic systems that can jam or disable satellites (none of which require nuclear warheads forbidden by the Outer Space Treaty)
Meink dismissed concerns about escalation, and claimed that public acknowledgment serves deterrence.
He refused to elaborate further, noting that specifics “would actually not benefit that deterrence.” 
The admission lands amid a broader US push to treat space as the next decisive warfighting domain. 
War Secretary Pete Hegseth has called space “the single most decisive battlefield of this century and the centuries to come” and declared that the US will “demand orbital dominance.” 
Trump’s costly sci-fi daydream [Golden Dome project ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/50782)has been touted as a global missile defense system with orbital interceptors and space-based lasers.
The project - targeted for 2029 - fits into the same aggressive vision.
At the same conference, Meink said the Space Force has achieved “flight ready” hardware for space-based interceptors that can bat down adversary missiles from orbit - a centerpiece of the Golden Dome initiative.
Russia and China have slammed the Golden Dome as militarizing outer space, and North Korea labeled it a “path to nuclear war in space.”
Russia also noted that its modern strategic nuclear systems – like the [hypersonic Kinzhal missile ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/67553)– could bypass such defenses.

🇮🇷⚡️ War Pushes Iran’s Energy Map North
Iran built most of its oil and gas system in the south, beside the Persian Gulf and the [Strait of Hormuz](https://t.me/newrulesgeo/2527). In peacetime, that was simply geography. In war, it becomes a vulnerability: fields, terminals and tanker routes all sit inside the same battlespace.
Tehran is now pushing north. Iran is returning the Amir Kabir semi-submersible rig to deep-water exploration in the Caspian after years of inactivity. The Iranian-built platform can operate in water almost 1,000 meters deep and drill 6,600 meters beneath the seabed. It was previously used to confirm oil at the Sardar-e Jangal structure.
Exploration is moving ahead in Block 18 and off Gilan, while seismic work in Golestan is expected to lead to another well next year.
The Caspian will not replace Iran’s giant southern fields any time soon. That is not the immediate point. Even modest northern production gives Tehran something money alone cannot buy: distance from the war in the Gulf.
Oil and gas produced there could supply Iran’s northern provinces and industry without being hauled across the country from the south. New drilling would support ports, service vessels, repair facilities and the same [domestic oil-sector expertise](https://t.me/newrulesgeo/2548) Iran is already developing elsewhere. A strike campaign focused on the Gulf coast would no longer threaten every part of the energy system at once.
The north also opens a different map. Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan lie across the Caspian. Iran could expand energy swaps with its neighbors and potentially send future Caspian crude to Kazakhstan, whose pipeline network already runs east toward China. The International North–South Transport Corridor gives Tehran another route connecting its northern ports to the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean.
None of this is a ready-made replacement for Hormuz. It is the beginning of a second network of fields, partners and transport routes that Washington would find much harder to squeeze at the same time.
Bringing Amir Kabir back also keeps deep-water drilling skills inside Iran. The rig was built domestically by Sadra; restoring it preserves the crews, marine support and repair base needed for future projects. Iran followed the same sanctions-driven path at its [first geothermal power plant](https://t.me/newrulesgeo/2536), adapting drilling methods and energy equipment at home.
The US-Israeli war was supposed to narrow Iran’s options. Instead, it is pushing Tehran to spread its energy system across two fronts and tie the northern one more closely to Eurasia.
The Caspian does not need to rival the Persian Gulf. It only needs to make Iran harder to isolate, blockade or cripple with a single campaign.

🇬🇧🇸🇦 Britain’s battered military eyes another Yemen misadventure
Saudi Arabia has asked Britain for diplomatic and military help against Yemen’s Ansar Allah forces as the Houthis push toward Bab el-Mandeb and attacks batter Saudi oil infrastructure, Bloomberg reported.
Riyadh wants operational support along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and help protecting oil facilities after its East-West pipeline was knocked offline. Britain has already agreed to send military advisers.
🏳️ The same Royal Navy whose own government says only around half of its surface fleet is at high readiness or above is now being eyed as backup for Riyadh. The Navy has even admitted that one Portsmouth store alone is sitting on 84,000 repairable items worth around £200 million after years of funding and maintenance problems.
📉 Britain’s armed forces are also markedly smaller than they were in 2022, while Army applications recently plunged by nearly a third year-on-year.
⚔️ Meanwhile, Ansar Allah’s advance and the Saudi pipeline shutdown have helped push Brent toward $110, with British officials privately warning that Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb could have a “catastrophic” effect on shipping and inflation.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband nevertheless declared:
💬 “I made clear that the UK stands firmly with Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized Government of Yemen.”
The rusting leftovers of Britain’s imperial military are already fantasizing about another Middle East misadventure.

☠️ Iran turns Pentagon’sEpstein Fury into an expensive embarrassment
The Pentagon’s first special report on Operation Epstein Fury quietly documents what [months of victory boasts ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/69306)could not hide: depleted ammunition stocks, wrecked aircraft, battered bases and a logistics network forced to retreat and improvise under Iranian fire.
💵 By June 29, the Pentagon already put the war’s cost at $33.4 billion: $22.3 billion in expended munitions and $3.7 billion in equipment losses — not including repairs to damaged infrastructure.
💬 The war caused “strategic inventory shortfalls” and exposed “industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply,” the report admits.
🚀 Iran damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases across eight countries. The Pentagon’s own table lists four F-15Es destroyed, an F-35A damaged, an A-10 destroyed, multiple KC-135 tankers hit, an E-3 damaged and as many as 30 MQ-9 drones destroyed.
📌 The humiliation spread to logistics. After Iranian strikes, US medical-evacuation helicopters were pulled from Iraq and Kuwait, leaving most evacuations to be carried out by ground, including local ambulances.
⛴ Iranian attacks also forced the Navy to shift sustainment away from Bahrain, while moving support to Diego Garcia stretched resupply cycles to 14–18 days. The report itself admits that establishing adequate naval bases and support ports posed “significant challenges.”
And after burning through men, missiles and machinery, [Hegseth](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74595) went back to Congress warning that without more money the Pentagon could face “critical shortfalls” threatening its ability to replenish weapons and sustain global operations.[ The White House asked for another $67.1 billion](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/71862) for the Pentagon, mostly for Epstein Fury.
